lines: fn scaled(self) -> Self where Self: Sized;
}  // dyn Shape works; scaled is not callable

items: `where Self: Sized` on a method excludes it from the vtable.
That rescues the rest of the trait.
On the trait itself it does the opposite — kills `dyn` entirely.

blocks.title: E0038
blocks.text: `the trait `Foo` cannot be made into an object`, with a note pointing at the exact offending method.

items: `Clone` is not object safe, so nothing built on it is.
For generic methods: take `&dyn OtherTrait` instead of `<T: OtherTrait>`.
That moves the erasure one level down.

blocks.q: When is object safety actually checked?
a_bullets: When you write `dyn Trait`, not when you define the trait.
A dyn-hostile trait is perfectly fine if only used generically.
So `Clone` and `PartialEq` are not broken — just not erasable.

blocks.title: Design For Both
blocks.text: Want a trait usable generically and as `dyn`? Keep methods `&self`-receiving, non-generic, and `Self`-free in their signatures.

caption.text: Part 4 of RUST FIELD GUIDE. Rust's trait system is one idea — a contract — wired into four different machines: generic bounds, monomorphization, vtables, and coherence. This handbook walks all of them, from `impl Trait for Type` through the orphan rule, object safety, associated types, and the blanket impls that quietly close your API forever. If you have ever stared at E0038, E0117 or E0119 and guessed at the fix, slide 10 is your lookup table.
